title: De Optimo Genere Oratorum
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

passages.original: oratorem genere non divido; perfectum enim quaero. Vnum est autem genus perfecti, a quo qui absunt, non genere differunt, ut Terentius ab Accio, sed in eodem genere non sunt pares. Optimus est enim orator, qui dicendo animos audientium et docet et delectat et permovet. Docere debitum est, delectare honorarium, permovere necessarium.
passages.english: I do not divide the orator into kinds, for I am seeking the perfect one. And there is only one kind of the perfect [orator]; those who fall short of him do not differ in kind, as Terence differs from Accius, but within the same kind they are not equal. For the best orator is the one who by speaking both instructs and delights and moves the minds of his hearers. To instruct is a duty owed, to delight is a gift freely given, to move is indispensable.
passages.notes: The opening sentence begins mid-thought ('oratorem genere non divido'). 'Debitum', 'honorarium', 'necessarium' play on financial and legal terms: what is owed, what is an honorary or voluntary payment, and what is necessary.

passages.original: ita fit ut Demosthenes certe possit sum misse dicere, elate Lysias fortasse non possit. Sed si eodem modo putant exercitu in foro et in omnibus templis, quae circum forum sunt, conlocato dici pro Milone decuisse, ut si de re privata ad unum iudicem diceremus, vim eloquentiae sua facultate, non rei natura metiuntur.
passages.english: So it comes about that Demosthenes can certainly speak in a low style, whereas Lysias perhaps cannot speak in an elevated one. But if they think that, with an army stationed in the forum and in all the temples around the forum, it would have been fitting to speak for Milo in the same way as if we were speaking on a private matter before a single judge, they are measuring the force of eloquence by their own ability, not by the nature of the case.
passages.notes: 'sum misse' is a scanning split of 'summisse'; 'exercitu' is read as such (ablative absolute with 'conlocato').

passages.original: quin ipsum Isocratem, quem divinus auctor Plato suum fere aequalem admirabiliter in Phaedro laudari fecit ab Socrate quemque omnes docti summum oratorem esse dixerunt, tamen hunc in numerum non repono. Non enim in acie versatur nec ferro, sed quasi rudibus eius eludit oratio. A me autem, ut cum maximis minima conferam, gladiatorum par nobilissimum inducitur, Aeschines, tamquam Aeserninus, ut ait Lucilius, non spurcus homo, sed acer et doctus cum Pacideiano hic componitur,—optimus longe post homines natos—.
passages.english: Indeed, even Isocrates himself, whom that inspired author Plato, his near contemporary, made Socrates praise admirably in the *Phaedrus*, and whom all learned men have declared to be a supreme orator, I nevertheless do not place in this number. For he does not engage in the battle line or with the sword; rather, his oratory plays as if with wooden foils. I, however, to compare the smallest things with the greatest, am bringing on the most celebrated pair of gladiators: Aeschines, like Aeserninus, as Lucilius says, "no filthy fellow, but keen and skilled," is here matched "with Pacideianus," "by far the best since men were born."
passages.notes: The quotations from Lucilius (Aeserninus and Pacideianus were famous gladiators) imply that Demosthenes is the Pacideianus of the pair; the passage breaks off before naming him. "rudibus": the *rudis* was the wooden practice sword used by gladiators. The text "laudari fecit" is unusual Latin for "caused to be praised"; some editions read "laudari fecit" or "laudare fecit" ("made Socrates praise"). The sense is the same either way.

passages.original: quorum ego orationes si, ut spero, ita expres sero virtutibus utens illorum omnibus, id est sententiis et earum figuris et rerum ordine, verba persequens eatenus, ut ea non abhorreant a more nostro—quae si e Graecis omnia conversa non erunt, tamen ut generis eiusdem sint, elaboravimus—, erit regula, ad quam eorum dirigantur orationes qui Attice volent dicere. Sed de nobis satis. Aliquando enim Aeschinem ipsum Latine dicentem audiamus.
passages.english: If, as I hope, I render their speeches by making use of all their excellences, that is, their thoughts and the figures of those thoughts and the order of the matter, while following the words only so far as they do not clash with our usage (and even if they have not all been translated from the Greek, we have nevertheless worked to make them of the same kind), there will be a rule by which the speeches of those who wish to speak in the Attic manner may be guided. But enough about myself. Let us at last hear Aeschines himself speaking in Latin.
passages.notes: 'expres sero' is a scanning split of 'expressero'. 'Quorum' (whose) refers back to the orators named before this passage, Aeschines and Demosthenes.
